To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Accurate genomic evaluation for young bulls and cows can be achieved with genotypes for 3,000-5,000 evenly-spaced SNP, selected from a common subset of SNP, and that this is more accurate than using a single set of SNP selected for each trait".
genomic evaluation of the dairy bull and cow populations can be achieved with single low-density genotyping assays containing about 3,000-5,000 evenly-spaced SNP.
the accuracy of genomic evaluations for milk production traits is high, even when using low-density SNP genotyping assays.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a low cost, high density SNP genotyping assay for the dairy cattle population.
the development and application of methods for the analysis of large-scale data sets, in particular in the field of molecular biology and genomics.
the use of genomic selection to predict breeding value in dairy cattle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genomic evaluation using low density assays is possible, and that the accuracy of genomic evaluation is not a limiting factor for genomic selection in dairy cattle.
the accuracy of genomic evaluation of dairy bulls and cows is not affected by the density of the SNP used to derive prediction equation.
the use of low density assays for genomic prediction in Holstein bulls is feasible, but that the accuracy is lower than that of high-density assays.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the accuracy of DVG predictions is very high, even when using a low-density genotyping assay, and that the use of a low-density SNP assay is justified for genomic selection of young bulls and cows.
the accuracy of genomic prediction of DGV in dairy cattle is high enough to be used in the breeding programs of most countries.
a single low-density assay containing 5,000 SNP is a reasonable choice for genomic selection in the Holstein breed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a common set of SNP is adequate for genomic evaluation across traits, and the choice of SNP is not critical.
the use of low-cost SNP assays in genomic evaluations of the broader population of cows and bulls is feasible, and the accuracy of DVG is only slightly reduced when compared to high-density assays.
it is possible to use a single genotyping assay that is inexpensive to perform to predict DGV for a wide range of traits in dairy cattle.
